title: About
text: This Quarto project is my personal website, designed to serve as hub for my academic work from EPPS 6302: Methods of Data Collection and Production. It’s primary purpose is to organize and present content related to the current course and my group project. The website is configured to provide a clean, modern, and user-friendly experience, with a clear navigation structure.

Part A: Modified the Web Scraping Program
Tools used: R and the packages rvest, tidyverse, stringr, scales
Data Source: [Wikipedia - List of countries by GDP (nominal)]

Changed the original starter code: Foreign Exchange Reserves to GDP (nominal) data from Wikipedia

Modified XPath selector through the Developer tools to target GDP table and updated column names to reflect the GDP data sources (IMF, World Bank, UN), and successfully scraped 230+ countries/territories

# =============================================================================
# PART A: Scrape GDP (nominal) table from Wikipedia
# =============================================================================

url <- 'https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal)'

# Read the HTML code from Wikipedia
wiki_gdp <- read_html(url)
cat("Successfully read HTML. Object class:", class(wiki_gdp), "\n")

Successfully read HTML. Object class: xml_document xml_node 

# Extract the GDP table using XPath
# The table is the second sortable table on the page
gdp_table <- wiki_gdp %>%
  html_nodes(xpath='//*[@id="mw-content-text"]/div[1]/table[2]') %>%
  html_table(fill = TRUE)

cat("Table extracted. Object class:", class(gdp_table), "\n")

Table extracted. Object class: list 

# Extract the dataframe from the list
gdp_df <- gdp_table[[1]]

# Assign meaningful column names
names(gdp_df) <- c("Country.Territory", "IMF.2025..1..6.", "World.Bank.2022.24..7.", "United.Nations.2023..8.")

cat("\nColumn names:", paste(colnames(gdp_df), collapse = ", "), "\n")

PART B: Clean up the dataframe

I attempted to clean and stripped all [1], [2], etc. reference brackets using regex “\\” and “[.*?\\]” but I do not think it worked correctly, I even try to get help from Copilot but it was unsuccessful at helping me removed them.
in B(ii), I successfully filtered the “World” aggregate row, handled the “NA” strings to proper R NA values, changed GDP columns from character to numeric, stripped commas from large numbers befire conversation


# =============================================================================
# PART B: Clean up the dataframe
# =============================================================================

## B(i): Clean up variables - Remove citation brackets and trim whitespace
cat("\n=== Cleaning Data ===\n")


=== Cleaning Data ===

gdp_clean <- gdp_df %>%
  # Remove citation brackets like [1], [2], etc.
  mutate(across(everything(), ~str_remove_all(., "\\[.*?\\]"))) %>%
  # Remove any extra whitespace
  mutate(across(everything(), trimws))

## B(ii): Remove unneeded rows and columns

# Identify and remove summary rows (World, rows with "—" as separators, etc.)
# The first row is typically "World" which is a summary
gdp_clean <- gdp_clean %>%
  filter(Country.Territory != "World") %>%
  filter(Country.Territory != "") %>%
  filter(!str_detect(Country.Territory, "^—"))

# Convert GDP columns from character to numeric
# First replace "NA" strings with actual NA, remove commas
gdp_clean <- gdp_clean %>%
  mutate(
    IMF.2025..1..6. = ifelse(IMF.2025..1..6. == "NA" | IMF.2025..1..6. == "", NA, IMF.2025..1..6.),
    World.Bank.2022.24..7. = ifelse(World.Bank.2022.24..7. == "NA" | World.Bank.2022.24..7. == "", NA, World.Bank.2022.24..7.),
    United.Nations.2023..8. = ifelse(United.Nations.2023..8. == "NA" | United.Nations.2023..8. == "", NA, United.Nations.2023..8.)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    IMF.2025..1..6. = as.numeric(str_remove_all(IMF.2025..1..6., ",")),
    World.Bank.2022.24..7. = as.numeric(str_remove_all(World.Bank.2022.24..7., ",")),
    United.Nations.2023..8. = as.numeric(str_remove_all(United.Nations.2023..8., ","))
  )

Part C: Data Collection Plan
A good data collection plan ensures your web scraping is legal, reliable, and reproducible. Here’s my approach and the key principles to considered when doing Web Scraping Research is:

Legal & Ethical Compliance

Before Scraping, the first is to plan the needed data, where to find it, and if scraping is allowed, we can do this through the robots.txt and Terms of Service, and how often the data is updated, and cite the source properly.

Data Quality Assurance
After scraping the quality of the data must be assurance through multiple ways which are run automatically through the code, easily creates professional tables, real validation of the data, and shows data quality that the scraping worked correctly:
i. Basic Validation Checks: Row Count Verification, Column completeness, Realistic values, No duplicates, Missing data count, Correct Data Count.
ii. Cross-Source Validation: to calculate the correlations between three key variables, to show how well the variables agree, prove data reliability for a correlation >0.99.
iii. Outlier Detection: identifies countries with >10% different between sources, Flags potential data quality issues, and shows which countries need closer examinations
iv. Reasonableness Checks: for descriptive statistics, confirms valies, and no negative or large values
v. Data Completeness Analysis: shows how many the subject of the data have all sources, categorizing for complete, mostly complete, limited, none, percentage breakdown
vi. Missing Data Patterns: Examples of the data subject with missing values, to help explain why there is data missing
Best Practices

For example, in my case Wikipedia allows for scraping for research purposes, I only made one requests for the GDP data, I did not made bulk requests for hundreds of pages, I believed it is cited properly. I did used Xpath, which can be found through the developer tools, to target the table and added error handling and quality checks the code to have for the right number of rows and columns.

text:
a. Biden-Xi summit data
The analysis of the Biden-Xi Summit Twitter data, discusses the meeting between the two presidents at the November 2021 summit, contained 14,220 rows, 90 columns. The text analysis was made using the Algorithmic Modeling Culture for pattern discovery using R tools of quanteda and ggplot2 to demonstrate nd plot the process of turning noisy social media data into quantifiable structure to draw insights on nature of conversation.
There are three key findings that provide structural connectivity in a heavy political discussion:
(1) The corpus had 58,080 documents or tweets and 63, 972 features or unique words, which explains the following the needed dimension reduction that was successfully completed by Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA). The LSA reduced the complexity to four latent dimensions/topics. This means the Biden-Xi Summit can be summarized in four underlying themes.
(2) The second finding is the Feature Co-occurrence Matrix (FCM) of the hashtags that were used to revealed a strong, quantifiable relationship between entities. The highest co-occurrence of 443 times was between #biden and #china. Similarly, the hashtags between country and leader: #china and #xijinping had a strong linkage.
(3) Influence and User Context: The three official accounts (@potus and @joebiden), and major media and news sources (@politico, @nytimes) are identified as the top entities in the conversation. The final piece of the code was the creation of a matrix (user_fm) to map which users were mentioned together to draw insights and understanding on the flow of political discourse.
b. US presidential inaugural speeches
This code analyzes the United States Presidential Inaugural Speeches using a variety of techniques (word clouds, KWIC/X-Ray Plots, frequency measures, and Keyness analysis) to track rhetorical changes over time and stylistic differences between leaders.

Any similarities and differences over time and among presidents?

Presidents became less likely to refer to the country as the “Union” and less likely to mention “Constitution” or “Foreign” countries. As time passed they were more likely to refer to the United States as “America” and more likely to mention “freedom” and “God.”
c. What is Wordfish? 
Based on the quanteda website, Wordfish is an unsupervised scaling model used to estimate the relative ideological or policy positions of texts/documents with a single, latent dimensions. Also, it is considered a Poisson scaling model that uses the maximum likelihood estimation to simultaneously determine both the estimated positions of the document and words (features) within the text. Wordfish does not require any assignment of policy position or reference scores. The only thing it needs is to set the orientation and document of the scale using two specific documents (e.g. dir = c(6,5))).
Learn more about WordFish: https://quanteda.io/articles/pkgdown/examples/plotting.html?q=wordfish#wordfish)

This Quarto project is my personal website, designed to serve as hub for my academic work from EPPS 6302: Methods of Data Collection and Production. It’s primary purpose is to organize and present content related to the current course and my group project. The website is configured to provide a clean, modern, and user-friendly experience, with a clear navigation structure.
Key Features and Structures:
Website Type: My Quarto is configured as a website, generating multiple HTML pages linked together with a consistent navigation bar.
Navigation Bar: The navigation bar is a central component, providing easy access to different sections of the site.
Left Side:

Home: Links to the main landing page of the site.
Group Project: Has a drop down menu providing access to details about the “Upcoming” group project.

Theme and Fonts: The sandstone theme provides a warm, natural color palette. Arial is used for the main text, with a larger font size of 1.5rem for enhanced readability. Courier New is used for code or monospaced text.
Link Color: Links are given a vibrant pinkish-purple color (#ff33f0) to stand out.
Custom CSS: An external stylesheet (styles.css) is included to allow for further customization beyond the built-in theme.

title: Assignment 2 Google Trends Analysis
text:
This is my analysis using Gtrend R package on the Google trends data using the keywords: Trump, Kamala Harris, and Election. The following charts shows the trends broken down by specific intervals: quarters and election cycles (dates) to create a direct comparison. The following results show the search interest for ‘Election’ and ‘Kamala Harris’ is cyclical, peaking only during election years (2021, 2022, 2024) meanwhile the search interest for “Trump remains consistently high through election and non-election years showing a distinct pattern of sustained public interest.
As mentioned above, I used two methods: (1) Continuous Date-Based Analysis (Dates) that shows search interested by monthly points and yearly in a timeline format and this method is best used to identify specific spikes during short term and overall trend, and (2) Interval-Based Analysis (quarters), this will focus on the search points by finding the averages and total value of the each election quarters or cycles. This method is best used to see long therm patterns of between non- and election years to create clear summary or analysis table.
As shown below:

Continuous Date-Based Analysis (Dates): The graphs use continuous scale (2021-01 to 2025-12) with data point at specific date to show the evolution of each search of both candidates and lines it with precise timing of the Election.












Interval-Based Analysis (quarters): These next graphs show the average election search by quarter and the non- and election search interests in a discrete aggregated time buckets by quarters and years using the categorical/discrete scale (e.g. 2020-Q3, 2024-Q3), the third quarter representing the election years, 2020 and 2024. This analysis helps simplify the data to facilitate comparisons between different time periods or quarters to highlight long term patterns, in this case “Off Year” vs “Election Year” averages and to create clear summary tables.

Difficulties encountered in scrapping the data:
(1) Inefficient Download Process: I had sequential downloading which resulted in mandatory 1-3 seconds delay for approximately 25 minutes for 722 files. I did not have anything to previously download files to keep from redundant downloads and wasted bandwidth. When I ran the code, the same files were downloaded multiple times (file #1 downloaded 3 separate times)
(2) Limited Error Recovery: I do not know a way to track progress which makes it impossible to monitor long-running downloads. The absence of resume capability means interruptions require starting from scratch. Non-specific error message because it only shows “filed to download” without diagnostic details.
(3) File Management Issues: The file path concatenation error creates malformed file names that could overwrite each other. There needs to be further or more advanced file size validation. Finally, I had limited future analysis because the metadata from JSON source is not preserved alongside PDFs.
Data Usability Assessment: The overall usability is moderate, files are accessible, but there is still some limitations to be able to have more contextual information for systematic analysis.

Successfully retrieved 722 valid PDF links from official government source.
All test downloads (10/10) completed without errors.
Data source (govinfo.gov) is authoritative and reliable.
File naming convention captures unique identifiers for tracking.

Recommended Improvements:

Fix file path constructing using file.path() to prevent naming errors.
Implement existence checking to skip already-downloaded files.
Export metadata CSV before downloading to preserve document context.
Add progress bar using progress package for visibility.
Enable parallel processing to reduce total by ~75%
Create structured download log capturing success/failure status, time stamps, and error messages
Implement resume functionality to continue from last successful downloads
